vignette: Mr. Tan is an 80-year-old widower with a rich history as a data scientist, whose life has been marked by both professional success and profound trauma. Now retired but still deeply engaged with his passion for numbers and analysis, Mr. Tan often reflects on the time he spent working as a relief worker in a war-torn region of Southeast Asia over 50 years ago. Despite the passage of time, the memories of that period continue to haunt him. He vividly recalls the relentless sound of gunfire mingling with the cries of civilians and the overwhelming sense of powerlessness that came from trying to provide aid amidst such chaos. These experiences have left deep emotional scars that persist even now in his elderly years. Mr. Tan's days are often disrupted by intrusive thoughts and flashbacks, particularly when he encounters anything that remotely reminds him of those traumatic events. The sound of fireworks on the Fourth of July sends him into a state of acute anxiety; the loud bangs instantly transport him back to the battlefield, where explosions were commonplace. During these episodes, he becomes disoriented and agitated, often pacing the floor or muttering incoherently. His nights are no less troubling. Mr. Tan experiences vivid nightmares that replay scenes from his time as a relief worker. He dreams of being trapped in a bombed-out building, frantically trying to help injured individuals but finding himself unable to reach them before it's too late. These nightmares leave him exhausted and often result in night sweats and increased heart rate. The impact of these symptoms extends beyond the psychological realm into his daily life. Mr. Tan has become increasingly isolated, avoiding social interactions for fear of encountering triggers that might set off a cycle of distressing memories. Even watching news programs or reading articles about conflict zones can be overwhelming, prompting him to withdraw from media entirely. This isolation has left him feeling disconnected from the world and from his community. His occupation as a data scientist, which once brought him great joy and fulfillment, now feels burdensome. The precision required in his work contrasts sharply with the unpredictability of his PTSD symptoms. He finds himself struggling to concentrate on complex datasets or analytical tasks, often getting distracted by intrusive thoughts about past traumas. Despite this, he continues to engage in data science as a way to maintain a semblance of normalcy and purpose. Mr. Tan also grapples with persistent negative beliefs and feelings related to his trauma. He often questions whether he could have done more to help those in need during the war zone relief work. These self-critical thoughts are compounded by a pervasive sense of guilt, as if his survival is somehow unworthy or undeserved. His relationship with his late wife was deeply impacted by these struggles. Though she was supportive and understanding, Mr. Tan sometimes felt like he was burdening her with his anxiety and emotional distance. This dynamic has left him feeling even more isolated in the years since her passing. In recent months, Mr. Tan has become increasingly aware of how his PTSD symptoms are affecting his daily life. He recognizes that his fear and avoidance behaviors are limiting his ability to enjoy simple pleasures and maintain meaningful connections with others. While he remains committed to finding ways to cope with his trauma, he is also seeking support from friends and community members who understand the unique challenges faced by those who have lived through such experiences. Through these ongoing struggles, Mr. Tan's resilience and determination are evident. His love for data science continues to provide a sense of structure and purpose in his life, even as he works to navigate the enduring impact of his wartime trauma.
